. The data covers a critical period in modern financial history, spanning the aftermath of the dot-com bubble, the 2008 global financial crisis, and the subsequent economic recovery
. The highest percent change of approximately 0.05 (or 5%) occurred around 2005-2006
, followed by a steep decline to near-zero levels
Treasury bills are short-term government debt securities, and their returns are highly sensitive to the Federal Reserve's benchmark interest rate
. The sharp decline in returns starting in 2007 and bottoming out near 0% from 2009 to 2015 reflects the Federal Reserve's 'Zero Interest Rate Policy' (ZIRP) implemented to combat the Great Recession
. Conversely, the peak in 2005-2006 corresponds to a period of monetary tightening where the Fed raised rates to cool an overheating economy
. The rise after 2015 indicates the beginning of the Fed's rate normalization cycle as economic conditions improved
For investors, T-bills represent the 'risk-free rate' of return

. During the 2009-2015 period, holding T-bills yielded virtually no nominal return (hovering between 0.03% and 0.08%), which forced conservative investors and pension funds to seek yield in riskier assets
. This prolonged near-zero return environment had significant social implications, particularly for retirees who relied on safe, fixed-income investments for their daily living expenses
The rapid rises and falls in the chart highlight how quickly government monetary policy can shift in response to macroeconomic shocks
